machine_translation_en: It soothes hot swellings, erysipelas, namla, pustules and ulcers, and what is on the palms, and fire burns, with oil; so does its wine (sharab), and its leaves applied as a plaster after being mashed with oil and wine; so do its oil and the ointments made from its oil. The dried plant helps when sprinkled on a whitlow, and so does the cerate made from it.
note: 'wa-ma kana ala al-kaffayn' is 'and what is on the palms', not 'including those on the palms'; 'zayt' is oil (olive oil only by assumption). Substance, scope and locator fine.
Faithful; 'abra'at' rendered 'heals' (allowed wording).
Scalp and ear (canal) ulcers with pus; dripping applies to the ear. Section 'head' correct.
Faithful. 'Everything said of myrtle' is a cross-reference: those myrtle uses must not be copied to acacia as separate claims.
Faithful. 'muhallaluhu' is probably a typo for 'mahluluhu' (its solution); 'its dried root' is odd for a gum resin (identification already disputed).

Faithful. The flesh-eating and stronger flesh-growing claims are attributed to isranj (red lead), a product of isfidaj; only 'fills ulcers, grows flesh' belongs to isfidaj itself. Lead: historical record only.
Faithful; 'foul wounds' (wasikha) as infection-like is within the agreed scope.

machine_translation_en: It removes tetters and grows blood [so the text; probably a copying error for 'flesh', al-lahm] in deep ulcers, especially with powdered frankincense. [Next section, joints:] it helps swellings of the muscles.
note: The Arabic has 'yunbitu al-dam' (grows blood); the machine translation silently emended it to 'flesh'. Mark the emendation. The joints clause is out of scope.
Faithful; 'ilk al-anbat' (Nabataean gum) is terebinth resin as in use_en. Baras/bahaq out of scope. Caustic copper salt: historical record only.
Only the burn use is asserted. The wound use is a reported view ('qad qila', it is said); keep it only with that label, never as a condition the Canon asserts. Broken bones out of scope.
Agree with reader: ulcer marks/scars, hair and cosmetic uses are out of scope. Translation also omits 'and sweat' (wa-l-araq) at the end.

machine_translation_en: It soothes swellings; its leaves are given to drink [so the text, yusqa; for burns probably a copying error for an external application] for carbuncle, fire burns and phlegmatic swellings; its juice with white lead is put on namla and erysipelas, and it is gargled for swollen tonsils.
note: The burn/carbuncle mode of use is doubtful in the OpenITI text; the translation must carry the doubt. Only the juice-with-white-lead clause is a clean external use. Check against an edition.

machine_translation_en: With honey it is put on a whitlow and it goes away; its husks are good for the marks of ulcers; with vinegar and oil [possibly a copying error for pitch, zift] as an embrocation it helps the pain called 'mrkb' [probably a corruption of murmakiya, Greek myrmekia, ant-like warts], a pain in the body like warts with a feeling like creeping ants.
note: 'murakkab' is not a disease name; the description matches myrmecia (ant warts). Only the whitlow clause is in scope; scars and warts are not.

Translation faithful. Caution: the reader's gloss of 'harfiyya' as 'harqiyya' (burn ulcers) is a conjecture and is redundant with the explicit burn-ulcer clause that follows; do not use 'harfiyya' as a burn claim.
Faithful; no preparation stated.

machine_translation_en: Good for malignant ulcers, 'Persian fire', chronic ulcers and deep wounds, and it is among the foremost remedies in these chapters; with Cimolian earth and white lead it helps when put on erysipelas.
note: 'mutaqaddim ma'a jumla' means 'foremost together with a group', not 'ranks first'; the original translation overstated the text.

Garbled (OpenITI MISSING_PARTS): section label 'al-jirah wa-l-quruh' with its colon corrupted to 'h'. 'jabal al-miskin' is probably 'habl al-masakin' (a name for ivy), which bears on the lablab identification. Section tagged 'cosmetics' in error.

machine_translation_en: [Begins mid-sentence:] ... for large abscesses (khurajat), cooked in wine, it closes them; as a plaster it helps fire burns, especially with a cerate, and for this it has no equal [la nazira lahu, written 'latazirlah' in OpenITI].
note: In scope, but the section field says 'cosmetics' (it belongs to the wounds-and-ulcers section, whose label was lost in span 14707). Identification risk: this matches the ivy (kissos) tradition and the 'habl al-masakin' fragment, not Lablab purpureus; flag the lablab identification as uncertain before use.
Faithful; the flesh-growing claim is only 'incidental' and Galen denies it: any use must carry the disagreement. Chafing (sahj) of groin and thighs is the clean claim. Lead: historical record only.
Agree with reader: general property ('prevents putrefaction'), not a wound use. Translation's ellipsis omits 'its astringency is its strongest action; it increases wind'.
Burn clause faithful; trailing comparison with borax (bawariq) correctly elided.

machine_translation_en: Its root kneaded with honey [and] bitter-vetch flour opens abscesses slow to ripen, and it is applied as a plaster. [Section: wounds and ulcers:] it dries wounds and joins them strongly, even a cut tendon; powdered with honey it is put on fire burns, wounds of the sinews and deep ulcers; mixed with bitter vetch and honey it cleans the dirt of ulcers.
note: The original translation read 'al-jirah wa-l-quruh:' twice (as object of 'plaster' and as section label); it is the section label. The span crosses from the swellings section into wounds-and-ulcers; the section field is only right for the first clause.

machine_translation_en: It fills ulcers with good flesh; its root helps scalds from hot water because it dries and cleans moderately, and so do its leaves cooked; and it closes (yudmil, object not stated); it is best used with rose oil.
note: 'wounds' was added to 'yudmil'. Identification risk: the entry distinguishes 'irsa' (iris, span 15906) from sawsan; the burn uses match the Greek lily (krinon) tradition, so sawsan here may be Lilium, not Iris.
Faithful. Same identification caution as 15904: 'the garden kind' of sawsan is plausibly the white lily.

[the rest of the clause is about food].

note: The last clause is corrupt in OpenITI; the original translation smoothed it into a confident reading. The by-mouth clause is internal.
